scenes.tts: The first film kept allele tiles separate while the phenotype changed. How can we follow those copies when people cannot be crossed for an experiment? We must use evidence that already exists, then match each question to the right scale. Each view can answer only some questions.

scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's color map exactly: red allele tile #E85D5D, pale allele tile #F4E7C5, B marker blue. Begin with the carried R/W tiles and phenotype lens. As schematic family portraits appear, transform R/W into generic D/d tiles labelled 'new family model'. Keep a small 'schematic' label visible.

scenes.visual: The family portraits join with thin lines while the title 'From Families to Chromosomes' writes briefly above them. Transform the title into a small header. The generic D and d tiles keep drifting inside the portraits.

scenes.tts: A pedigree turns a family into a model. Squares and circles stand for people, and shading marks the chosen trait. Lines connect partners and children. Generations stack downward, letting a pattern unfold through time. The shape is a symbol, not a genotype.
scenes.caption: A pedigree turns a family into a model. Squares and circles stand for people, and shading marks the chosen trait. Lines connect partners and children. Generations stack downward, letting a pattern unfold through time. The shape is a symbol, not a genotype.
scenes.visual: Transform each portrait into a large square or circle without changing its position. Draw partner lines, then child lines, then lower generations. Shade one symbol only after a small legend 'shaded = shows trait' appears.
scenes.narration: A pedigree turns a family into a model. Squares and circles stand for people, and shading marks the chosen trait. Lines connect partners and children. Generations stack downward, letting a pattern unfold through time. The shape is a symbol, not a genotype.

scenes.tts: The parents do not show the trait, yet their child does. Which simple model fits this clue better: dominant or recessive? Hold both possibilities beside the family before you decide.
scenes.caption: The parents do not show the trait, yet their child does. Which simple model fits this clue better: dominant or recessive? Hold both possibilities beside the family before you decide.
scenes.visual: Center two unshaded parent symbols above one shaded child. Place equal-size cards 'dominant?' and 'recessive?' on either side. Keep both cards neutral. Generic D and d tiles move faintly behind the symbols without revealing a pairing.
scenes.narration: The parents do not show the trait, yet their child does. Which simple model fits this clue better: dominant or recessive? Hold both possibilities beside the family before you decide.

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction question. Both model cards remain neutral and equally bright. The family lines breathe gently and a thinking ring turns once. Do not mark either model correct or rejected.

scenes.tts: A recessive model can fit. Each unshaded parent may carry a recessive allele, and the child may receive both copies. This pattern points toward recessive inheritance, but a small family does not prove it. The parents are carriers in this simple model.
scenes.caption: A recessive model can fit. Each unshaded parent may carry a recessive allele, and the child may receive both copies. This pattern points toward recessive inheritance, but a small family does not prove it. The parents are carriers in this simple model.
scenes.visual: Move one pale d tile from each unshaded parent into the shaded child. Brighten 'recessive can fit' but do not cross out the dominant card. Add 'clue, not proof' beside the family. Keep all uncertainty wording on screen.
scenes.narration: A recessive model can fit. Each unshaded parent may carry a recessive allele, and the child may receive both copies. This pattern points toward recessive inheritance, but a small family does not prove it. The parents are carriers in this simple model.

scenes.tts: Geneticists test a model against every person, not a striking branch. A dominant trait usually appears in each generation, and a shaded child usually has a shaded parent. A new DNA change can be an exception. A small family can still fit several explanations.
scenes.caption: Geneticists test a model against every person, not a striking branch. A dominant trait usually appears in each generation, and a shaded child usually has a shaded parent. A new DNA change can be an exception. A small family can still fit several explanations.
scenes.visual: Expand the carried pedigree to three generations. Sweep a soft highlight through every person as a checklist fills. Show a schematic dominant pattern with 'usually' labels, then add one neutral question badge labelled 'possible new change'.
scenes.narration: Geneticists test a model against every person, not a striking branch. A dominant trait usually appears in each generation, and a shaded child usually has a shaded parent. A new DNA change can be an exception. A small family can still fit several explanations.

scenes.tts: Alleles remain separate, and each genetic tool reveals a different scale. A pedigree works at the family scale. It can test inheritance models, but it cannot show the allele copies directly.
scenes.caption: Alleles remain separate, and each genetic tool reveals a different scale. A pedigree works at the family scale. It can test inheritance models, but it cannot show the allele copies directly.
scenes.visual: Pull a bracket around the whole pedigree labelled 'family scale'. Fade the moving allele tiles into dotted outlines to show that they are inferred, not seen. Keep the trait shading solid because phenotype is observed.
scenes.narration: Alleles remain separate, and each genetic tool reveals a different scale. A pedigree works at the family scale. It can test inheritance models, but it cannot show the allele copies directly.

scenes.tts: Now zoom from a person into a cell with a nucleus. A karyotype sorts photographed chromosomes into matched pairs by size and shape. It answers questions about whole chromosomes and large changes. Matched partners make an extra or missing copy visible.
scenes.caption: Now zoom from a person into a cell with a nucleus. A karyotype sorts photographed chromosomes into matched pairs by size and shape. It answers questions about whole chromosomes and large changes. Matched partners make an extra or missing copy visible.
scenes.visual: Zoom through one pedigree symbol into a large schematic cell, then its nucleus. Chromosome bars condense and sort into 22 matched autosome pairs plus one sex pair labelled 'XX or XY'. Put '46 total' on screen, never in narration. Label the sorted view 'whole-chromosome scale'.
scenes.narration: Now zoom from a person into a cell with a nucleus. A karyotype sorts photographed chromosomes into matched pairs by size and shape. It answers questions about whole chromosomes and large changes. Matched partners make an extra or missing copy visible.

scenes.tts: An extra chromosome is large enough to count. A single gene, such as the ABO gene, is far too small to identify here. The picture can reveal scale-sized changes, not every inherited detail. A karyotype cannot identify a person's ABO alleles.
scenes.caption: An extra chromosome is large enough to count. A single gene, such as the ABO gene, is far too small to identify here. The picture can reveal scale-sized changes, not every inherited detail. A karyotype cannot identify a person's ABO alleles.
scenes.visual: Add a third bar at chromosome pair 21 and change the on-screen total from 46 to 47. Label 'trisomy 21'. Then shrink a labelled 'ABO gene' dot below visible resolution and place 'not visible on a karyotype' beside it.
scenes.narration: An extra chromosome is large enough to count. A single gene, such as the ABO gene, is far too small to identify here. The picture can reveal scale-sized changes, not every inherited detail. A karyotype cannot identify a person's ABO alleles.

scenes.tts: Nearly every body cell with a nucleus carries the same DNA and genes. Skin and muscle cells differ because they use different gene sets. Mature red blood cells lose their nuclei, leaving no chromosomes to count.
scenes.caption: Nearly every body cell with a nucleus carries the same DNA and genes. Skin and muscle cells differ because they use different gene sets. Mature red blood cells lose their nuclei, leaving no chromosomes to count.
scenes.visual: Transform the same chromosome set into side-by-side schematic skin and muscle cells. Different groups of gene-label lights glow in each. Transform a third cell into a mature red blood cell as its nucleus fades away.
scenes.narration: Nearly every body cell with a nucleus carries the same DNA and genes. Skin and muscle cells differ because they use different gene sets. Mature red blood cells lose their nuclei, leaving no chromosomes to count.

scenes.tts: Start with the question, then choose the view. Use a cross for possible allele combinations, a pedigree for family patterns, and a karyotype for whole chromosomes. No view can answer every genetics question. Match the tool to the scale of evidence.
